passages.happening: God tells Ezekiel to ask Pharaoh, ‘Who can be compared to your greatness?’ (verse 2). Then he points to Assyria: ‘Look at Assyria, a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches that shaded the forest. It towered on high; its top was among the clouds’ (verse 3). The deep waters made it grow (verse 4). ‘All the birds of the air nested in its branches, and all the beasts of the field gave birth beneath its boughs; all the great nations lived in its shade’ (verse 6). ‘No tree in the garden of God could compare with its beauty’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The oracle is dated to about June 587 BC, while Babylon besieged Jerusalem. Pharaoh Hophra had sent an army that briefly drew the Babylonians away, and the hope that Egypt could save Judah was real.

The comparison was fresh. Assyria had been the great power for much of three centuries and had destroyed Samaria in 722 BC. Yet its capital Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC.

The cedars of Lebanon were the prize timber of the ancient world, and a great tree was a common picture of royal majesty, a world tree sheltering all creatures. Daniel tells of a dream given to Nebuchadnezzar about such a tree. This one is rooted in the deep, the waters beneath the earth, and grows in Eden, the garden of God.
passages.later: Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a tree in whose branches ‘the birds of the air nested’ (Daniel 4:12). Nahum announced, ‘Nineveh is devastated’ (Nahum 3:7).
passages.asks: The cedar sheltered all the nations and still fell. Ask whether you have mistaken greatness for permanence. And ask what lasting shelter looks like.

passages.t: Cut down, a warning to Pharaoh
passages.happening:
‘Since it became great in height and set its top among the clouds, and it grew proud on account of its height’ (verse 10), God handed it over to the ruler of the nations (verse 11). Foreigners cut it down, and its branches lay broken in every valley; the nations left its shade (verse 12). This was so that no other well-watered tree would ever again grow proud of its height (verse 14).

When it went down to Sheol, God made the deep mourn and Lebanon grieve, and the trees of Eden were comforted in the depths of the earth (verses 15-16). ‘Who then is like you in glory and greatness among the trees of Eden? You also will be brought down’ (verse 18). ‘This is Pharaoh and all his multitude’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The ruler of the nations is best taken as Babylon, which brought Assyria down and now raises its hand against Egypt. Sheol was the Israelite name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a pit beneath the earth. To lie among the uncircumcised was a particular shame for Egyptians, who practiced circumcision.

The last verse turns the whole poem on Pharaoh: if Assyria fell, so will you.
passages.later: Isaiah pictured the trees of Lebanon rejoicing over a fallen king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:8). Daniel's tree was cut down for the same pride (Daniel 4:14).
passages.hard:
Egypt was not destroyed like Assyria. Did this prophecy fail?

Egypt did survive as a nation, and the prophecy should be read on its own terms. The chapter is a poetic warning about Pharaoh's pride, cast in the language of a felled tree and a descent to Sheol. Babylon did defeat Egypt's ambitions in Asia; a Babylonian text records a campaign by Nebuchadnezzar against Egypt around 568 BC; and Egypt never again became the great power it had been, falling later to Persia. Some readers see this as the substance of fulfillment. Others note that oracles against the nations use sweeping, conventional imagery, and that Ezekiel himself later recorded an unexpected turn about Tyre (29:17-20), which suggests the prophets did not treat such oracles as fixed timetables. Either way, the point the chapter presses, that Egypt was no safe refuge, proved true.
passages.asks: The poem asks Pharaoh, who is like you? Ask where you have compared yourself to others and come out on top. And ask what it would mean to measure yourself before God.
